. The present appeal was preferred by the appellant on 08.02.2017 and was assigned to the then learned FSSA Court and after administrative directions vide order no. 12072-12106/ Judl.
/NDD/PHC/ND dated 01.10.2019 it was assigned to this court for disposal of the same as per law.

2. By way of present appeal, the appellant Dev Raj herein has challenged the judgment dated 30.01.2017 and order on the point of sentence dated 03.02.2017 passed by the then learned And vs Food Inspector on 2 March, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/77428885/
1 ACMM-II, PHC, New Delhi vide which the appellant/accused was held guilty for commission of offences punishable under sections 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act & Section 16(1)(a) r/w Section 7 of PFA Act,
1954, the appellant was awarded sentence to undergo Simple Imprisonment for 01 year with fine of Rs. 25,000/- for commission of aforesaid offences and in default of payment of fine to undergo Simple Imprisonment of 15 days.
3.

sentences.text:
The complaint was then filed in the court on 09.02.2011 alleging violation of Section 2(ia)(a)(b)(c) and (m) of PFA Act as punishable under Section 7/16(1A) of PFA. Act.
4.
The appellant was summoned by the learned trial court vide order dated 09.02.2011 for 09.05.2011.

After filing appearance, the appellant did not opt to move an application under section 13(2) of the PFA Act thereby exercising his right to get the second counterpart of the sample analyzed from the Central Food Laboratory (CFL).
5.

On the basis of evidence available on record, on 20.07.2011 charge was framed against the appellant/accused for commission of offences punishable u/s 7/16(1A) PFA Act for violation of Section CA no. 29/2017 Dev Raj Vs. Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 3 of 13 2(ia)(a)(b)(c) and (m) of PFA Act, alleging therein that on 01.11.2010 at about 07:00p.m., appellant being the Vendor cum Proprietor of M/s Aggarwal Sweets Corner at B-6/114, Sector-8, Rohini, Delhi sold for analysis approximately 1500 grams of 'Besan Ke Ladoo' taken from an open tray lying there, having no label declaration, meant for human consumption to Sh.Virender Singh, Food Inspector in presence of SDM/LHA and witnesses and accordingly it was analyzed by by the Public Analyst vide report dated And vs Food Inspector on 2 March, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/77428885/
2 24.11.2010 bearing No. PFA/Enf./3107/2010 and found that the sample of 'Besan Ke Ladoo' was adulterated because it was containing added vegetable oil which was not declared as an ingredient and thereby violated the provisions of sub clause (a)(b)(c) & (m) of Section 2(ia) punishable u/s 16(1)(a) of PFA Act, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
6.

Thereafter matter was listed for evidence, wherein prosecution examined PW-1 Sh. Ajay Kumar,
SDM Saraswati Vihar, the then SDM/LHA, Food Inspector, PW-2 Sh.Virender Singh and PW-3 Sh.S.N. Jindal, FA 6.1

During trial after the examination and detailed cross examination of three witnesses of the department, prosecution evidence was closed and matter was fixed for Statement of accused.
7.

The statement of appellant/accused was recorded under section 313 Cr.PC in which he pleaded his innocence and stated that sample proceedings were not conducted in his presence ; ladoos were prepared by the workers of the shop and at that time they put some vegetable oil in preparation of laddos so that they do not stick CA no. 29/2017 Dev Raj Vs. Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 4 of 13 to the tray ; there is no investigation about his status of appellant/accused in the firm M/s Aggarwal Sweets Corner ; the consent for prosecution was granted without application of proper mind ; no efforts were made to join public witnesses ; PA report is wrong and representative sample was not taken and present case is a false case.
He did not prefer to lead evidence in his defence.

7.1 After hearing the arguments of both the parties, the appellant/accused was convicted by the learned trial court for commission of offence punishable u/s 7/16(1)(a) PFA Act for violation of Section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, 1954.

8. The learned trial court in its impugned judgment dated 30.01.2017 observed that i) there is no witness who was present at the time of manufacturing of he commodity or who had seen any worker applying vegetable oil on the tray as a lubricant, therefore, there is no evidence in the form of testimony of any witness which could establish that the vegetable oil found by the PA in the sample was on account of such use of oil as a lubricant ;
ii) the samples had been collected according to the prescribed procedures from the premises of Vendor cum Proprietor ; on analyzing the sample commodity, it was found to be adulterated food,
not of the quality, nature or substance which he represented to be and thereby he committed the violation of Section 2(ia)(a) punishable u/s 7/16(1)(a) PFA Act.
The appellant was accordingly convicted and sentenced by the learned trial court and aggrieved by the said judgment and order CA no. 29/2017 Dev Raj Vs. Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 5 of 13 on quantum of sentence dated 03.02.2017, the present appeal has been preferred by the appellant.
9.(I) The appellant has assailed the judgment and order on sentence passed by the learned trial court by urging various grounds.
II) Alternatively, on the quantum of sentence, relying upon the new legislation, it was pleaded that the case of the appellants be considered sympathetically in the light of the preposition of law laid And vs Food Inspector on 2 March, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/77428885/
3 down by the Hon'ble Courts pursuant to coming of new legislation that is Food Safety & Standards Act.
10.

During the course of argument on 02.03.2021, learned counsel for the appellant submitted that appellant is not challenging the merits of the case/ conviction decided by the learned trial court vide judgment dated 30.01.2017 and is confining appeal limited to the quantum of sentence only awarded vide order dated 03.02.2017 ; and to affirm submissions, appellant tender his affidavit duly sworn and notarized by the Oath Commissioner, in this regard and prayed that a lenient view be taken against him by giving the benefit of New Legislation as FSSAI.
11.

Learned counsel for the Delhi Admn./Food Department, objected to the same and submitted that according to submission of appellant, prosecution has established its case and he be sentenced with strict punishment in terms of old Act wherein minimum punishment is prescribed and no leniency should be shown to the convict as it is a serious offence of food adulteration article / commodity leading to hazardous consequences on the health or CA no. 29/2017 Dev Raj Vs. Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 6 of 13 body of a person.
12.

I have carefully gone through the available record as well as trial court record, have heard the submissions of learned counsel for both the parties at length and have also gone through the judgments relied upon by the parties.

13. In light of above submissions and discussion particularly when the affidavit of appellants to this effect was filed on record, I find no valid and legal reasons to interfere with the well reasoned judgment of the learned trial court.
The findings of the learned trial court with respect to the conviction of the appellant for the offence punishable under 16(1A) of the PFA Act read with Section 7 of the PFA Act, 1954 are upheld.
II. Now Coming to the alternate plea of giving benefit of new legislation to the appellant/ accused.
14. It is argued by learned counsel for the appellant that on the date of pronouncement of judgment/order on sentence, the PFA Act, 1954 was repealed and new act has thereafter come into operation.

It is stated that the court should give benefit of the new legislation to the accused vide which the punishment provided under the old act has been diluted to a considerable extent, and that the offence for which the accused/appellant has been convicted now falls under the category of Substandard Food punishable under section 51 of the new Act i.e Food and Safety Standards Act,
2006 (hereinafter called FSSA) punishable with fine only upto 5 lakhs.
15.

It was argued by learned counsel for the appellant that appellant is a man of 42 years of age,
working as a salesman in the CA no. 29/2017 Dev Raj Vs. Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 7 of 13 bakery and getting salary of Rs.12,000/- per month ; married, having two children ; respectable person and has deep roots in the society, have responsibility towards family and not involved in any other case,
have left the said business and prayed that a lenient view be taken against him in the light of the provisions of law under the new Act.

4 15.1

Further it is stated that case pertains to the year 2011, the appellant/accused has faced the trial almost 10 years which by itself is a sufficient punishment and, the hardships faced by him has caused great mental agony, stress and rigors of trial during the said period.
It is also prayed that considering the family status and responsibilities of appellant his case be considered in special circumstances and a lenient view be taken against him.

It is also stated that now a days special circumstances exists due to outbreak of pandemic of Covid-19 and there are chances of appellant being infected with virus in case imprisonment of sentence is awarded to them.

15.2 In support of his submissions qua the consideration of the case under new legislation, learned counsel for appellant had relied upon the judgment of Nemi Chand Vs. State of Rajasthan ( Crl.
Appeals No. 214 and 215 of 2016, vide order dated 10.03.2016, as corrected vide order dated 17.03.2016, as reported in 2016 (1) FAC 203 ) of Hon'ble Supreme Court and earlier judgment T Barai Vs. Henry 1983 ( ) SCC 177.
15.3

Nemi Chand Vs. State of Rajasthan ( Crl.
Appeals No. 214 and 215 of 2016

sentences.text: Per contra, learned SPP, strongly opposed the submissions advanced by learned counsel by addressing that the sentencing CA no. 29/2017 Dev Raj Vs. Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 8 of 13 cannot be done in new Act since the definition of many offences have changed in the new Act including this particular offence of which accused is charged.

entities.text: CA no. 29/2017 Dev Raj Vs. Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 8 of 13
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Definition of major offences like "adulteration" and "misbranding" have been changed.
Now FSSAI have definition "substandard food", "food containing extraneous matter" "unsafe food" and misbranded food".

Due to this reason,
the ingredients have changed and thus there is no way in which the old offences could be related to new offences.
15.4 In the present case, the offence was that the food article i.e. Besan Ke Ladoo was found adulterated.
This was in violation of Section 2(ia)(a) of the PFA Act and thus consequently punishable under section 16(1)(a) of PFA Act read with Section 7 of PFA Act.

15.5 Sub-clause (viii) of 3(zz) FSSA Act is applicable where the colouring material or the preservative other than that specified in respect there of is found in the food article and not where the colouring material exceeds the prescribed limit.
15.6 Herein is a case different.

The Food article which was not of the quality,
nature or substance which he represented to be which in my considered opinion falls under the definition of 'substandard' as defined in section 3(zx) of FSSA.
AND the violation thereof is punishable under section 51 of the Act, whereby a penalty of fine only extended upto Rs. 5 lacs, is provided.

15.7 Another aspect may also be noted is that in terms of provisions of Rule 30 in certain category of cases falling under clause (c) of Rule 29 i.e. strawberrys, pierrce, cherry, jams, glazed fruits etc.,
permissible food colours limit is extended upto 200 ppm.
CA no. 29/2017 Dev Raj Vs. Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 9 of 13
Thus, drawing the analogy, it can not also be said the presence of synthetic colour of 149.85 ppm in the case at hand per se is unsafe and injurious to health.
15.8 Further, the charge in this case was framed for the said offences and there is no charge in which it is stated that the said adulteration was injuries to health.

Had it been the case, the charge would And vs Food Inspector on 2 March, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/77428885/
5 have been for the offence punishable u/s 16(1-A)(ii) of PFA Act r/w section 2(ia)(l) & (f).
15.9 Thus, it is held that it is the ingredients which constitute an offence and determines whether it is the same offence but with new name or an altogether different offence,
Here the offence of adding colour in the food article which was punishable u/s 16(1)(a) PFA Act is similar to the offence u/s 51 of FSSAI Act, which is now punishable with fine only upto five lakhs.
15.10 Now, coming to the application of Nemi Chand Judgment (supra), the same is based on the old judgment i.e. T Barai ( Supra) of Hon'ble Supreme Court.

The relevant portion of the T Barai Judgment is as follows :
- (Para 25) It is settled both on authority and principle that when a later statute again describes an offence created by an earlier statute and imposes a different punishment or varies the procedure, the earlier statute is repealed by implication in Michell Vs.
Brown ( 1958) 120 ER 909, 912 : 32 LTOS 146:7 WR 80 Lord Campbell put the matter thus :
- "It is well settled rule of construction that, if a later statute again describes an ofence created by a former statute and affixes a CA no. 29/2017 Dev Raj Vs. Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 10 of 13 different punishment, varying the procedure, the earlier statute is repealed by the later statute see also Smith Vs. Benabo ( 1937) 1 ALL ER 523 : ( 1997) 1 KB 518: 156 LT 194"
- In Regina Vs. Youle ( 1861) 158 ER 311,315-16 : LT 299 : 9 WR 637 Martin B. said in the oft-quoted passage :
- If a statute deals with a particular class of offences, and a subsequent Act is passed which deals with precisely the same offence, and a different punishment is imposed by the later Act, I think that, in effect, the legislature has declared that the new Act shall be substituted for the earlier Act."
- The rule is however subject to the limitation contained in Article 20(1) against ex post facto law providing for a greater punishment and has also no application where the offence described in the later Act is not the same as in the earlier Act i.e. when the essential ingredients of the two offences are different.
- Moreover, this particular aspect is stated as a illustration in the same judgment in Para 23 which is as follows :

- To illustrate, if Parliament were to reenact Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code,
1860 and provide that the punishment for an offence of murder shall be sentence for imprisonment for life instead of the present sentence of death or imprisonment for life, then it can not be that the courts would still award a sentence of death even in pending cases.

And vs Food Inspector on 2 March, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/77428885/
6 15-A - Academic Reference can also be made to the letter dated 03.10.2017 of Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, produced before the court during the proceedings.

entities.text: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
entities.label: ORG

sentences.text:
Vide said letter CA no. 29/2017 Dev Raj Vs. Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 11 of 13 the said authority, in the light of judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Nemi Chand's Case (supra) issued an advisory to the Commissioners of Food Safety/Officers incharge of Food Safety to dispose of the long pending court cases filed under old PFA Act mainly concerning substandard and misbranding by imposing fine only.
15-B - In view of the above mentioned discussion, it can be safely said that while considering the point of sentence, in backdrop of the object and reasons of the act and the intention of the legislature, the quantum of sentence so passed in the interest of justice needs to be considered under the new Act i.e. FSSAI, while deciding the present appeal.

16. Thus, analyzing the facts of the case, taking note of the special circumstances of the appellant/accused and the fact that appellant/accused has faced the trial of almost 10 years, in light of the above cited judgment and the judgment of Hon'ble High Court of Delhi titled as GNCT Vs.
Jagdish Tyagi dated 11.10.2017 in my view the convict/ appellant is entitled to the benefit of new legislation.

Accordingly, to meet the ends of justice, the sentence of the convict imposed by the learned trial court vide order dated 30.01.2017 stands modified to the extent that the order sentencing the appellants to undergo simple imprisonment of one year stands waived off ; the sentence of fine imposed upon appellant/accused enhanced from Rs. 25,000/- to Rs. 75,000/- In default of payment of fine the appellant/convict shall undergo simple imprisonment for two months.
Sentence modified accordingly.

CA no. 29/2017 Dev Raj Vs. Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 12 of 13 17 Appellants/Convict is directed to deposit the fine amount within 30 days from the date of pronouncement of this judgment before the learned trial court and, if any, amount of fine was deposited by the appellant before the learned trial court same shall be adjusted accordingly.
18.
